confidence_notes: Both user-supplied examples are SUBMISSION cover letters, not published correspondence and not point-by-point responses. The genuinely journal-specific part is CONTENT ASSERTIONS, not layout: Science enumerates nine required items, Cell four required plus three optional, Nature calls the letter optional but names it the confidential channel, Brain imposes a hard 323-character summary, JAMA requires full postal contact, PNAS does not ask for one at all, and eLife requires one only in five specific circumstances. Layout is stated by NOBODY: the two real letters disagree on font (Arial 10 pt vs Times New Roman 12 pt), margin (0.5 in vs ~0.9 in) and justification (justified vs ragged-right), so any house layout SUNA ships is SUNA's own opinion and must be recorded as such. PROVENANCE CAVEAT: www.science.org and www.cell.com both return HTTP 403 to direct fetch (Cloudflare), so the Science and Cell Press quotes were captured from indexed search results rather than a fetched page; the URLs are correct and the wording is consistent across sibling journals, but they should be re-read from the live pages in a browser session before shipping as profile data. The Nature Portfolio referee-suggestion sentence was captured from Communications Physics. That gap is now CLOSED with a negative answer: on 2026-08-19 nature.com/nature/for-authors/initial-submission returned HTTP 200 and was read in full. The three cl.nature.* cover-letter quotes reproduce VERBATIM from it, so they stay `documented`; the flagship page contains no referee-suggestion sentence at all (its only referee mention about the letter is that it 'is not shared with the referees'), which is recorded as cl.nature.reviewers-vehicle = null / not-stated. The commsphys sentence must NOT be generalised to the nature profile. eLife's author guide now lives at elife-rp.msubmit.net (elifesciences.org/author-guide 404s), a URL that looks like submission-system infrastructure and may move. SOURCE PATHS: SUNA_EXAMPLES/ holds only the user's original binaries (.docx/.pdf). anatomy.notes: The author decides 'this is what goes out' and gives that state a human-readable identity. Today the identity IS the filename: subject + date + optional time + optional status word or destination.

DOCX when the sender wants marks back; PDF when the sender wants it read, not edited. The word 'assembled' in one filename is itself evidence that the outbound artifact is a CONCATENATION of parts that live separately during authoring.
Email. dc:creator and cp:lastModifiedBy on the OSA file name two DIFFERENT people, one file passed hand to hand. THE RECIPIENT DOES NOT HAVE SUNA — the hard constraint on the whole design.

FOUR channels, simultaneously, in real files: w:comment records; w:ins/w:del tracked changes; highlight-as-assignment; and instructions written in prose INTO the body. Channels three and four carry the same information as a comment thread — an assignee and an open state — in a form no schema captures.

Several marked-up copies come back, overlapping. The OSA file is the visible product of a human manually merging two colleagues' feedback into his own copy by pasting it into his own comment threads, prefixed with the speaker's name.
The returned file is anchored to a FROZEN version; the working tree has moved on. Re-anchoring is against a MOVED target.
Every returned item acquires an owner and a status. Skipped by a solo author.
Edit the prose, reply in the thread, and quote the changed passage back.
Word carries this as w15:done on the commentEx record — the one field of the four that round-trips losslessly.

The next named artifact. Nothing in either consecutive freeze records that they are related, or what changed between them. The co-author who gets round N+1 has no way to learn what happened to round N's comments.

confidence_notes: NO PUBLISHER STATES ANYTHING ABOUT THE INTERNAL LOOP, so everything here except the four OOXML rules is counted-empirically from the user's own files. The most important negative finding: an internal round report DOES NOT EXIST in current practice. There is no artifact in any of the examples that tells a co-author what happened to their previous round's comments, so if SUNA produces one it is SUNA's invention and there is no shape to imitate — which is an argument for making it entirely DERIVED (so it cannot go stale) rather than an argument against building it. Four questions are genuinely unanswered by any source and are carried into the ADR as open decisions: what a version IS mechanically, whether returned binaries belong in git, retention for output artifacts, and which identifier is canonical for a co-author across Word, git and authors.json.
